title: The first two crewed spacecraft to meet in orbit came within 30 cm of each other

cover.alt: Colour film still: the side of a Gemini spacecraft lit by the Sun against black space, seen at close range from another spacecraft.

body: Gemini 6 was meant to meet an uncrewed Agena rocket in orbit, but on 25 October 1965 the Agena apparently exploded about six minutes after launch. NASA gave the crew a new target: the crewed Gemini 7. After one launch attempt ended on the pad, Wally Schirra and Tom Stafford took off on 15 December and caught up with Frank Borman and Jim Lovell in orbit, the **first crewed rendezvous**. For hours the two craft flew in formation, at times as close as one foot (30 cm).

slides.alt: Colour film from a spacecraft window: another Gemini capsule hangs nose-on against black space, then a close-up shows its side, lettered United States, gliding past.
slides.caption: Onboard film from the rendezvous, December 1965: one Gemini seen from the other, first nose-on, then close enough to read “United States” on its side.

slides.heading: How Gemini 6 got a new target

steps.label: Oct 1965: the Agena target is lost
12 Dec: engines stop 1.5 s after ignition
15 Dec: launch, and the two meet

slides.question: When the engines cut out on 12 December, why didn’t Gemini 6 astronaut Wally Schirra pull the ejection handle?
options: He felt no movement, so it hadn’t lifted
Mission Control told him not to
slides.explanation: He knew the rocket had not left the pad. His call probably saved the mission, since the Gemini ejection seats were of questionable reliability.

slides.label: the closest the two spacecraft came to each other
slides.text: Schirra said he could move to within inches of Gemini 7 “in perfect confidence”. One stretch of formation flying lasted 5 hours 19 minutes.

slides.prompt: During the flight, the Gemini 6A crew played a tune in orbit. What was it?
slides.detail: Played on an eight-note harmonica and a handful of small bells. The Smithsonian, which displays them, calls them the first musical instruments played in space.
